sections.heading: Process & CPU
bullets: OS — Operating System: manages hardware resources and provides services to programs
PCB — Process Control Block: kernel struct storing all process state (registers, PID, state, open files)
PID — Process ID: unique integer identifier for a running process
PC / IP — Program Counter / Instruction Pointer: address of the next instruction to execute
SP — Stack Pointer: points to the top of the current stack frame
ISA — Instruction Set Architecture: hardware-visible interface (e.g. x86, ARM, RISC-V)
LDE — Limited Direct Execution: run process directly on CPU while OS retains control via traps + timer IRQs
syscall — System Call: user process requests OS service by triggering a software trap
IRQ — Interrupt Request: hardware signal to the CPU to handle an event
ISR — Interrupt Service Routine: kernel function that handles an interrupt
IVT — Interrupt Vector Table: maps interrupt numbers to their handler addresses

sections.heading: Scheduling
bullets: FIFO / FCFS — First In First Out / First Come First Served: simplest scheduling policy
SJF — Shortest Job First: optimal turnaround, non-preemptive, requires knowing job length
STCF — Shortest Time-to-Completion First: preemptive version of SJF
RR — Round Robin: each job runs for a fixed time slice, great for response time
MLFQ — Multi-Level Feedback Queue: approximates SJF using past behavior
CFS — Completely Fair Scheduler: Linux default, uses red-black tree + vruntime
vruntime — Virtual Runtime: CFS measure of CPU time consumed, weighted by niceness
SQMS — Single-Queue Multiprocessor Scheduling: one shared queue for all CPUs
MQMS — Multi-Queue Multiprocessor Scheduling: one queue per CPU with work-stealing

sections.heading: Memory
bullets: VA / VPN — Virtual Address / Virtual Page Number: address seen by user-space code
PA / PFN — Physical Address / Physical Frame Number: actual DRAM address
MMU — Memory Management Unit: hardware translating VA→PA on every memory access
TLB — Translation Lookaside Buffer: hardware cache of recent VA→PA translations
ASID — Address Space ID: TLB tag per process, avoids full TLB flush on context switch
PTE — Page Table Entry: maps a VPN to a PFN plus metadata bits
PT — Page Table: per-process array of PTEs indexed by VPN
PDE — Page Directory Entry: top-level entry in a multi-level page table
CR3 — Control Register 3 (x86): holds physical address of the page table root
COW — Copy-On-Write: share frames read-only between processes; copy only on first write
OOM — Out Of Memory: kernel kills processes when all memory is exhausted
LRU — Least Recently Used: evict the page not used for the longest time

sections.heading: PTE / TLB Bits
bullets: Valid (TLB): this TLB slot holds a usable mapping (0 = unused slot)
Present (PTE): page is in physical RAM (0 = on disk → triggers page fault)
Dirty: page has been written and must be flushed to disk before eviction
Reference / Accessed: page was recently accessed; used by the clock algorithm
Protection: encodes read / write / execute permissions for the page

sections.heading: What is a Process? (Ch. 4)
bullets: A process = a running program — the OS abstraction of a CPU
Address space: the memory the process can address (code, stack, heap)
Machine state: PC, SP, general-purpose registers — everything needed to resume
OS creates a process: load code from disk → allocate stack + heap → init I/O (stdin/stdout/stderr) → jump to main()

sections.heading: Process States
bullets: Running: currently executing on the CPU
Ready: runnable but waiting for the CPU to be assigned
Blocked: waiting for I/O or an event (disk read, network, sleep)
Zombie: finished but parent hasn't called wait() yet — entry remains in process table
Running → Ready: preempted by scheduler (timer interrupt)
Running → Blocked: issued a blocking syscall (e.g. read())
Blocked → Ready: I/O completes, event arrives
Ready → Running: scheduler picks this process next

sections.heading: Process API (Ch. 5)
bullets: fork(): creates child as near-exact copy of parent. Returns child PID to parent, 0 to child, -1 on error
wait() / waitpid(): parent blocks until child terminates; cleans up the zombie entry
exec(): replaces the calling process image with a new program — never returns on success
Shell pattern: fork() → exec() in child, wait() in parent — used for every command you type
Zombie process: child that exited but whose status hasn't been collected by parent

sections.heading: Limited Direct Execution (Ch. 6)
bullets: Goal: run processes at full CPU speed while the OS retains control
User mode: process runs, cannot issue privileged instructions
Kernel mode: OS runs, full hardware access
System call: process executes trap → CPU switches to kernel mode → jump to IVT handler → return-from-trap
Timer interrupt: hardware fires periodically → OS preempts current process and can switch
Context switch: save current process registers to PCB → restore next process registers from PCB → return-from-trap
Cost: ~1–10µs per context switch; TLB flush on switch is the biggest overhead

sections.heading: Metrics (Ch. 7)
bullets: Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time (measures performance / throughput)
Response time = first run time − arrival time (measures interactivity)
The trade-off: optimizing turnaround (run to completion) hurts response time and vice versa
FIFO: simple, bad if long jobs arrive first (convoy effect)
SJF: optimal turnaround, needs job length upfront, non-preemptive
STCF: preemptive SJF, optimal turnaround but poor response time
Round Robin: excellent response time, poor turnaround (stretches all jobs)

sections.heading: MLFQ (Ch. 8)
bullets: Rule 1: If Priority(A) > Priority(B) → A runs
Rule 2: If Priority(A) = Priority(B) → A and B run in Round Robin
Rule 3: New job enters at the highest priority queue
Rule 4: Job uses full time allotment at a level → demoted to lower queue
Rule 5: After period S → boost all jobs to top queue (prevents CPU-bound starvation)
MLFQ approximates SJF/STCF without needing job lengths upfront
Anti-gaming: count total CPU time at a level, not just per-slice (can't reset by issuing I/O)
Parameters: number of queues, time slice per queue, boost period S

sections.heading: Linux CFS (Ch. 9)
bullets: CFS tracks vruntime per process and always picks the process with the lowest vruntime
Data structure: red-black tree ordered by vruntime — O(log n) insert/remove, O(1) min
nice value −20 to +19: lower nice = higher priority = slower vruntime increase
vruntime_delta = actual_time × (weight_0 / weight_of_process)
Target latency: every runnable process runs at least once per scheduling period
Sleeping process: removed from tree; on wake-up vruntime set to current min (avoids burst)

sections.heading: Multiprocessor Scheduling (Ch. 10)
bullets: Cache affinity: prefer running a process on the same CPU it last ran on (warm cache)
Bus snooping: caches monitor bus; on write, other caches' copies are invalidated
SQMS: one global queue for all CPUs — simple but lock contention + no cache affinity
MQMS: one queue per CPU — scalable + affinity, but needs work-stealing for balance
Work stealing: idle CPU peeks at another CPU's queue and steals jobs if imbalanced

sections.heading: Address Space (Ch. 13)
bullets: Every pointer printed in user code is a virtual address — never physical
Two processes can share the same virtual address (0x1000) mapping to different physical frames
Address space layout (low → high): Code → Heap (grows up) → [free] → Stack (grows down)
Goals of virtual memory: transparency, efficiency (hardware TLB), protection (isolation)

sections.heading: C Memory API (Ch. 14)
bullets: malloc(size): allocates size bytes on the heap, returns pointer (or NULL on failure)
free(ptr): returns the allocation back to the allocator — must free exactly once
sbrk() / brk(): syscall to grow the heap (move program break upward)
mmap(): maps files or anonymous memory — used for large allocations by malloc
Common bugs: memory leak (forget free), use-after-free, double-free, buffer overflow

sections.heading: MMU & Base+Bounds (Ch. 15)
bullets: MMU (Memory Management Unit): hardware inside the CPU chip that translates VA→PA on every access
Interposing: transparent layer between requester and resource — you write VA, hardware silently uses PA
Base+bounds: physical = virtual + base, if virtual ≥ bounds → segfault
OS sets base/bounds registers on each context switch (stored in PCB)

sections.heading: Segmentation (Ch. 16)
bullets: Each logical segment (code, heap, stack) gets its own base+bounds pair
Segments placed independently in physical memory
Code segment can be shared (read-only) across processes
Out-of-bounds: hardware detects offset ≥ bounds → raises SIGSEGV
Problem: external fragmentation — gaps between segments too small to reuse

sections.heading: Free Space Management (Ch. 17)
bullets: Free list: linked list of free chunks; each chunk has an embedded header (size + next pointer)
malloc: find chunk ≥ N in free list, split if needed; free: insert back and coalesce
Internal fragmentation: wasted space inside an allocation (allocated 16 bytes, needed 9 → 7 wasted)
External fragmentation: free memory exists but in non-contiguous pieces too small for the request
Coalescing: on free(), merge adjacent free blocks to prevent fragmentation
Best Fit: smallest chunk that fits — low internal waste but slow and causes small leftover fragments
First Fit: first chunk that fits — fast but fragments the beginning of the list
Slab allocator (Linux): pools of fixed-size objects (PCBs, inodes) — zero fragmentation for kernel objects

sections.heading: Paging Basics (Ch. 18)
bullets: Pages: virtual address space divided into fixed-size chunks (typically 4KB)
Frames: physical memory divided into same-size chunks
VA = [ VPN | Offset ] — VPN indexes into page table to get PFN
Physical address = PFN × page_size + offset
Page table: per-process array of PTEs — one PTE per virtual page
PTE bits: Valid, Present, Dirty, Reference, Protection, PFN
No external fragmentation (all chunks same size); simple allocation (any free frame works)

sections.heading: Page Table Math
bullets: Offset bits = log₂(page_size) — e.g. 4KB pages → 12 offset bits
VPN bits = VA_bits − offset_bits — e.g. 32-bit VA, 12 offset → 20 VPN bits
Number of PTEs = 2^(VPN_bits) — e.g. 2^20 ≈ 1 million entries
Page table size = entries × bytes_per_PTE — e.g. 2^20 × 4B = 4MB per process
Physical base of frame: PFN × page_size — e.g. PFN=5, 4KB → 5 × 4096 = 20480

sections.heading: TLB (Ch. 19)
bullets: TLB: hardware cache of recent VPN→PFN translations, inside the MMU
TLB hit: hardware reads PFN directly — no extra memory access — very fast
x86 TLB miss: hardware walks page table automatically (hardware-managed)
MIPS/RISC-V TLB miss: raises trap → OS handler loads entry (software-managed)
TLB entry: VPN | PFN | Valid | Protection | Dirty | ASID
Fully associative: any VPN can be in any slot; all slots searched in parallel
Typical TLB size: 32–128 entries; thrashing if working set > TLB coverage
Valid (TLB) vs Present (PTE): Valid = TLB slot is usable; Present = page is in RAM

sections.heading: ASID & Context Switch
bullets: Without ASID: flush entire TLB on every context switch (all Valid bits = 0)
With ASID: tag each TLB entry with process ID — no flush needed on context switch
ASID is stored in a special hardware register; OS sets it on each context switch
CR3 (x86): hardware register pointing to the physical address of the page directory root

sections.heading: Multi-Level Page Tables (Ch. 20)
bullets: Problem: single-level page table wastes memory for sparse address spaces
Solution: break the page table into pages — only allocate what is actually used
x86-32 two-level: VA = [PD Index | PT Index | Offset]; CR3 → Page Dir → Page Table → PFN
Advantage: sparse address spaces use very little memory
Cost: TLB miss requires 2–4 memory accesses instead of 1
Huge pages (2MB/1GB): fewer TLB entries needed; Linux THP promotes them automatically

sections.heading: Swap Space (Ch. 21)
bullets: Swap space: reserved disk area for pages that don't fit in physical RAM
Enables address spaces larger than physical memory — disk is ~100,000× slower than RAM
Present bit = 0 in PTE → page is on disk; PTE stores the swap offset (disk address)
Page fault flow: Present=0 trap → OS reads swap offset → I/O to load page → update PTE → retry instruction

sections.heading: Page Replacement Policy (Ch. 22)
bullets: OPT / Bélády: evict the page used farthest in the future — optimal but requires future knowledge
LRU: evict the page not used for the longest time — best practical policy
Clock (Second-Chance): approximates LRU with a circular list and reference bit
Clock algorithm: ref=1 → clear it and move on (second chance); ref=0 → evict
Dirty page: must be written to disk before eviction; clean page can just be discarded
Dirty bit set by hardware on any write to the page

sections.heading: Eviction & Thrashing
bullets: High/low watermark: OS starts evicting when free frames < low watermark; stops at high watermark
kswapd: Linux background daemon that proactively evicts pages to maintain the low watermark
Thrashing: OS spends more time swapping than doing useful work — working set > physical RAM
OOM killer: Linux kills a process when all memory + swap is exhausted to free frames
Working set: set of pages actively used by a process — must fit in RAM to avoid thrashing

sections.heading: Copy-On-Write (COW)
bullets: fork() uses COW: child and parent share all physical frames marked read-only
First write by either process → protection fault → OS copies only that one page → mark writable
If child calls exec() immediately after fork(), almost no pages are actually copied — very fast
COW also used by: mmap(MAP_PRIVATE), shared libraries, VM snapshots

sections.heading: Linux Address Space Layout
bullets: Virtual address 0 is intentionally unmapped — null pointer dereference raises SIGSEGV (loud failure)
64-bit user space: 0x0000000000000000 → 0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF
64-bit kernel space: 0xFFFF800000000000 → 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
Kernel is mapped into every process's address space at high addresses — no TLB flush on syscalls
BSS segment: uninitialized global/static variables, zeroed by OS at program load

sections.heading: Linux Scheduling Classes
bullets: SCHED_NORMAL: normal user processes, uses CFS
SCHED_RT: real-time processes with hard latency requirements (SCHED_FIFO or SCHED_RR)
SCHED_IDLE: lowest priority background tasks
CFS nice range: −20 (highest priority) to +19 (lowest priority)

sections.heading: mmap & Memory Mapping
bullets: mmap(MAP_SHARED): maps a file into memory; writes go directly to the file and are visible to all mappers
mmap(MAP_PRIVATE): COW mapping — writes create process-private copies, original file unchanged
Anonymous mmap: not backed by a file — used by malloc for large allocations
munmap(): unmaps a region and frees its virtual address space

sections.heading: Cache Coherence & Locality
bullets: Temporal locality: recently used data will likely be used again — justifies keeping it in cache
Spatial locality: data near a used address will likely be used soon — justifies cache line granularity
Bus snooping: multi-CPU cache coherence — when CPU A writes an address cached by CPU B, CPU B's copy is invalidated
MESI protocol: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid — common cache coherence protocol

sections.heading: Address Bit Formulas
bullets: offset bits = log₂(page_size)  →  4KB page: log₂(4096) = 12 bits
VPN bits = total_VA_bits − offset_bits  →  32-bit VA, 4KB: 32 − 12 = 20 bits
Number of page table entries = 2^(VPN_bits)  →  2^20 ≈ 1 million
Page table size = 2^(VPN_bits) × bytes_per_PTE  →  2^20 × 4 = 4 MB
Physical address = PFN × page_size + offset

sections.heading: Worked Examples
bullets: 16-bit VA, 512B pages: offset=9 bits (2^9=512), VPN=7 bits (16−9), 128 PTEs
32-bit VA, 4KB pages: offset=12 bits, VPN=20 bits, 1M PTEs, page table=4MB
32-bit VA, 8KB pages: offset=13 bits, VPN=19 bits, 512K PTEs, page table=2MB
VA 0x0001F3AC, 4KB pages: offset = 0x3AC (low 12 bits), VPN = 0x1F = 31
PFN=5, page_size=4096: physical base = 5 × 4096 = 20480
Multi-level (10|10|12): VA=0x00401010 → PD=1, PT=1, offset=0x010
